title: Routing congestion scenario mitigation cheatsheet
body:
Summary:
This is a compact investigative playbook for diagnosing and mitigating routing-congestion symptoms we see when serving MoE-enabled variants of Llama/Mistral/Qwen at long contexts (16k–64k). It collects quick repro steps, lightweight profiling commands, heuristics that worked in staging, and an operational runbook for emergency mitigation. The objective: minimize SLO impact (p95/p99 tail latency) while preserving throughput and model quality.

Symptoms observed (representative):
- Latency spikes at tail for requests with long prefix + dense routing fanout (p99 increases 2–6x).
- High GPU-side stall cycles with low SM utilization but high PCIe DMA / host->GPU memcpy activity.
- Per-request expert fanout skew: small subset of experts receive >70% of tokens.
- Queueing/backpressure in worker threads; RPC latency variance across NUMA domains.

Environment notes to capture when reproducing: model name + size (eg llm-llama-70b-moe, mistral-large-experts), seq length distribution, batch window target, hardware (A100-80GB, H100), NIC/PCIe topology, and kernel build (cuda/cudnn/driver). Always capture peak active experts count and per-expert memory usage.

Repro recipe (fast local):
1) Use scripted generator that emits mixed-length requests: 20% long (>=32k), 80% short (<=512).
2) Pin to single server with deterministic routing seed.
3) Run at 60–80% client qps and capture traces.

Suggested lightweight profiling commands: (start here before heavy profiling)
- Collect runtime traces: RUNTIME_TRACE=1 ./serving_binary --trace-file traces.pb
- GPU utilization and memcpy hotspots: nvidia-smi dmon + nvprof sampling for 1 minute window.
- Python/Torch stack: python -m torch.profiler (with record_shapes=False to reduce overhead).
- Kernel scheduling: perf record -g -p <pid> for host-side locks and thread stalls.

Key diagnostics to extract:
- Per-token routing table: fraction of tokens that hit top-10 experts.
- Inter-expert message sizes and number of DMA submissions per forward pass.
- Time split: gating computation, routing serialization, collective/expert compute, memcpy.
- Queue depth histogram for each expert worker thread.
- NUMA-locality of input tensors and resulting PCIe hops.

Common causal patterns (ranked by frequency in our runs):
1) Skewed gating distribution + dense long prefixes -> very uneven expert load, causing hot experts and increased queuing/serialization cost.
2) Small request fragmentation: many small fragments cause many small DMA ops (high overhead) instead of fewer big transfers.
3) Cross-NUMA traffic: host staging buffers live on a different NUMA node than the worker thread, causing PCIe hops and odd memcpy stalls.
4) Synchronous prefetch/handshake that blocks worker threads waiting for KV cache availability.
5) Aggressive batching heuristics that increase latency variance when a hot expert appears.

Mitigation strategies (fast to try in order):
- Short-term emergency: enable model fallback to dense variant for requests longer than threshold (e.g., >24k) or when active-expert-skew > threshold. This preserves latency at cost of compute.
- Smooth gating: apply temporary temperature or top-k gating cap so no more than N experts are chosen per token (N=2–4). This reduces fanout.
- Fragment coalescing: increase minimum fragment size / aggregate fragments per-request to reduce DMA op count.
- Soft admission control: limit per-request expert tokens inflight; queue earlier at ingress and shed lower-priority requests.
- NUMA affinity: bind expert worker threads to NUMA node of prefetch buffers; pin host staging buffers accordingly.
- Backpressure tuning: lower max_batch_window_ms for suspected hot-expert endpoints to reduce queueing.

Longer-term engineering fixes:
- Dynamic expert rebalancer: periodic small-weight transfers to pull load off hot experts (background, low-overhead).
- Asynchronous prefetch pipeline decoupled from synchronous handshakes; prefetch uses bounded worker pool with token priority.
- Coarse-grained expert coalescing on-device: group small expert tensors into larger contiguous blobs to reduce transfer count.
- Routing-aware scheduler: prefer colocated experts in the same GPU/node for a request when possible.

Microbench results that motivated fixes (example runs):
- Baseline: llm-llama-70b-moe, 32k context, 8 servers (A100): p95=420ms, p99=2.1s, hot-expert share=78%.
- After gating-cap N=3 + fragment coalescing: p95=180ms, p99=470ms, throughput -10%. Quality delta (perplexity): +0.8% measured on small eval set.
- After NUMA affinity + async prefetch prototype: p99 down to 320ms, hot-expert share reduced to 55%.

Checklist for an incident (rapid runbook):
1) Toggle dense fallback for the affected deployment and observe SLOs for 2 minutes.
2) If fallback not acceptable, apply gating-cap and coalescing flags (runtime flags feature-flag/gating-cap).
3) Move ingress traffic to another region/cluster if capacity headroom exists.
4) Collect traces (runtime traces, nvprof) and attach to JIRA.
5) Notify oncall (runtime-ops) and schedule a follow-up postmortem.

When to escalate to infra/research:
- If p99 remains >2x pre-incident after emergency mitigations.
- If root cause indicates a hardware-level DMA serialization defect or driver-level bug (capture driver versions and open a ticket).

Open questions / experiments to validate:
- Does gating temperature scheduling per-session (not per-token) reduce oscillation?
- Can we use a cheap Learned Routing Prior (LRP) to bias tokens away from hot experts dynamically with negligible quality impact?
- Quantify trade-offs of fallback to dense at different context lengths — run A/B with real traffic.

Notes to reviewers: this doc is deliberately pragmatic; it is an ops-first playbook intended for SREs and runtime engineers. Add any quick flags, script snippets, or command shortcuts you used during incident triage to the linked_artifacts list.

Appendix: quick flags we use in staging (examples):
--routing-gating-cap=3
--enable-fragment-coalesce=true
--fragment-coalesce-min-bytes=262144
--dense-fallback-context-threshold=24576
--prefetch-async-worker-pool=8

(End of cheatsheet)
